His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected.
